## Booking a Meeting Slot {-}

Book your group's seminar meeting in the online planner:

[Book a meeting slot](https://terminplaner.dfn.de/public/bookings/30d3a64c-356c-4dc3-82ca-a02fd46df1c0){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank" rel="noopener"}

::: {.spaced-list}
* **One slot per group per week.** Each slot takes up to three participants, and all of them must belong to the same group. Every group member who attends signs up for the same slot. Do not join a slot that a member of another group has already booked.
* **Monday slots: in person or online.** You choose whether we meet in room HB-108 or via Zoom. After booking, send an email to [dominik.liebl@ku.de](mailto:dominik.liebl@ku.de) stating which option your group wants.
* **Tuesday slots: online only.** All Tuesday meetings take place via Zoom. No email is needed.
:::

All online meetings take place in this Zoom room:

[Join the Zoom meeting](https://kuei.zoom-x.de/j/66424019307){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank" rel="noopener"}

Victor Frankenstein did not fail because his creation was weak. He failed because he brought it to life without understanding it, and then walked away.

Statistical methods are no different. Software makes it easy to stitch together an estimator, a test, and a p-value, and throw the switch. But a method applied without understanding its assumptions, mechanics, and failure modes will sooner or later turn on its user.

{{{< include _stats-monster.qmd >}}}

::: {.tagline}
Become knowledgeable users of statistical methods.<br>
Otherwise, they become your monster.
:::

In this seminar, you take one statistical method into the lab: you dissect it, bring it to life in code, and deliberately make it fail using Monte Carlo simulations. You leave the lab as its master, not its victim.

---

## Lab Protocol {-}

::: {.spaced-list}
1. **Equip the lab.** In the first meetings, we learn together how to build Monte Carlo simulations that make statistical methods fail (@sec-mc).
2. **Assign the specimens.** Each lab group gets one statistical method (@sec-topics).
3. **Dissect it.** Work out its assumptions, its mechanics, and how it turns on its users. Write it all up in your seminar thesis (@sec-thesis).
4. **Present it.** Show your creature to the seminar, including the moment it turns on you.
::: 
-->

## Seminar Rules {-}

* **Groups:** two to three students each.
* **Grading:**
    * 80% seminar thesis
    * 20% presentation, in which *every* group member speaks.
* **Seminar thesis:**
    * **Length:** 8–12 pages main text, including figures and tables; title page, table of contents, references, and appendix do not count.
    * **Format:** PDF with 12 pt font, 1.5 line spacing, and 2.5 cm margins. The thesis templates (@sec-thesis) already meet these requirements.
    * **Code:** Only short snippets in the main text. Submit the full code separately so that all results can be reproduced (fixed random seed).
    * **Submission:** `thesis.pdf` and a ZIP file of your complete thesis folder (text, code, and literature). Deadline: TBA.
* **Exam registration (via [campus.KU](https://campus.ku.de/)) deadline:** January 21.

## Groups and Topics {-}

The groups are formed, and each group has its topic:

| Group | Topic |
|:--|:--|
| 1 | Linear & Ridge Regression Analysis |
| 2 | Nonparametric Density Estimation |
| 3 | (Multiple) Testing |

⚠️ Being assigned to a group does not replace the official course and exam registration via [campus.KU](https://campus.ku.de/).
